addressed_problems.content: The study's findings are limited to ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 backbones, supervised ImageNet and self-supervised simCLR and MoCo pre-training objectives, iterative unstructured magnitude pruning (IMP) with a fixed 20% pruning ratio per round, and a specific rewinding point (5% of training). It remains unresolved whether other backbone families (e.g., Vision Transformers, EfficientNets), alternative self-supervised objectives (e.g., BYOL, SwAV, Barlow Twins), different IMP schedules (e.g., varying pruning ratios, alternative rewinding points, or one-shot pruning), or structured pruning schemes (e.g., channel pruning, filter pruning) yield similarly matching subnetworks with comparable sparsity thresholds, mask properties, and universal transferability to downstream tasks. Establishing this generality is crucial for understanding the robustness of the lottery ticket hypothesis in computer vision pre-training and for broadening its practical applicability.

Although the paper identifies unstructured sparse matching subnetworks (up to 96.48% sparsity on some tasks) and observes that MoCo-derived masks exhibit more kernel-level clustering (i.e., more completely pruned kernels) which may favor hardware speedups, it does not evaluate actual end-to-end training or inference speedups on realistic hardware platforms. The practical runtime implications of these unstructured sparse subnetworks remain unknown: it is unclear whether the observed sparsity levels and kernel-clustering patterns translate into measurable latency reductions on processors such as CPUs, GPUs, or mobile accelerators (e.g., using XNNPACK for smartphone inference). Future work must assess whether the identified subnetworks yield practical acceleration without performance degradation, and whether structured pruning—explicitly noted as a future direction—is required to achieve hardware-friendly efficiency.

The supplementary experiments reveal significant variability in the transfer success of pre-training-derived winning tickets across object detector architectures. For instance, while YOLOv4 accepts transferred subnetworks from MoCo, ImageNet, and simCLR pre-training with little performance loss at moderate sparsity, Faster R-CNN and SSD detectors often fail to preserve performance when using the same transferred masks—particularly for simCLR pre-training, where the subnetworks are no longer matching. The authors acknowledge that this discrepancy may stem from framework-specific implementation sensitivities (PyTorch vs. TensorFlow) or from inherent architectural differences between one-stage and two-stage detectors. The precise interplay between detector design (e.g., anchor-based vs. anchor-free, region proposal mechanisms, feature pyramid structures) and the transferability of pre-training-derived masks is not yet understood, leaving open the question of how to reliably select or adapt subnetworks for diverse detection pipelines.

The paper characterizes universal transferability of pre-training winning tickets to downstream classification, detection, and segmentation tasks, but only on datasets of moderate scale and spatial complexity (e.g., CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, Pascal VOC). The sparsity levels at which transferred subnetworks remain matching vary substantially: for example, 86.58–91.41% sparsity for natural image classification, 59.04–67.23% for synthetic VisDA2017 classification, and 36.00–83.22% for Pascal VOC detection/segmentation depending on pre-training method. It remains unresolved whether these subnetworks retain their matching property when transferred to very large-scale downstream tasks (e.g., full ImageNet classification, COCO detection/segmentation) or tasks requiring stronger spatial reasoning (e.g., video object detection, instance segmentation in the wild, depth estimation). Characterizing the limits of sparsity for universal transfer across more demanding tasks would reveal whether the lottery ticket phenomenon in pre-trained computer vision models scales to real-world deployment scenarios.

While the paper provides ablations on pre-training scale (ResNet-50 vs. ResNet-152 for simCLR) and temperature hyperparameter for simCLR, it does not establish systematic principles for selecting pre-training and pruning hyperparameters that optimally produce universally transferable matching subnetworks. For example, the observed interaction between pre-training method, sparsity level, and downstream task domain (natural vs. synthetic) suggests that no single recipe works universally: supervised ImageNet pre-training yields better transfer to synthetic data at moderate sparsity, while self-supervised methods (simCLR, MoCo) excel on natural images at extreme sparsity. Furthermore, the temperature scaling factor for simCLR affects transfer accuracy only outside a moderate range ([0.1, 0.5]), but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. A principled framework for choosing the pre-training objective, model scale, pruning schedule, and hyperparameters (e.g., temperature, rewinding point) to guarantee universal transferability is still lacking, representing a concrete direction for future investigation.

Deep computer-vision practice increasingly relies on large pre-trained convolutional networks (supervised ImageNet pre-training or recent self-supervised methods such as simCLR and MoCo) as general-purpose initializations for diverse downstream tasks (classification, detection, segmentation). Training and then fine-tuning very large pre-trained models is computationally expensive, and the community lacks principled means to reduce the size of a pre-trained model while guaranteeing that the smaller model will retain transfer performance across varied downstream tasks. Prior model-compression work in vision typically compresses a model after task-specific training and does not ensure universal transferability of the compressed model. Separately, the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) has shown that, at random initialization or early in training, sparse matching subnetworks ("winning tickets") can be trained to match dense-model performance; recent NLP work found transferable winning tickets in BERT pre-training. However, it is unknown whether analogous matching subnetworks exist when the initialization is a pre-trained CV model (supervised or self-supervised), whether such subnetworks can transfer universally across heterogeneous downstream vision tasks, and how different pre-training objectives, pruning schedules, or pre-training model scales affect the existence, structure, and robustness of these subnetworks. This absence of evidence leaves practitioners without a validated pathway to (a) amortize pre-training cost by producing compact, universally transferable initializations, and (b) understand whether LTH observations extend to the multiplicity of CV pre-training regimes and downstream tasks that impose different architectural priors (e.g., equivariances required by detection versus invariances used in classification).

nodes.content: In the context of LTH research, previous demonstrations of matching subnetworks largely addressed random initializations or early-training rewinding, and the NLP community recently reported transferable winning tickets in BERT pre-training. For computer vision, however, pre-training admits a diversity of popular objectives (supervised ImageNet classification, contrastive self-supervision like simCLR and MoCo), and convolutional architectures differ fundamentally from transformer-based language models. The specific question unresolved prior to this work was whether the act of pre-training a convolutional backbone produces an initialization that itself contains sparse subnetworks which, when retained and trained in isolation, match the performance of the full pre-trained network on the same pre-training objective. Without evidence of such pre-training winning tickets, one cannot justify pruning at the pre-training stage as a viable route to storage or computational savings that preserve pre-training-task performance.

Practitioners frequently pre-train a large backbone and then fine-tune it on many classification targets; doing so with the full pre-trained model can be costly at scale. Classical compression pipelines focus on compressing a model for a single target task after fine-tuning, which does not ensure the compressed model will be reusable across tasks. Prior LTH transfer studies addressed transfer between related classification tasks but did not study the combination of (a) multiple pre-training objectives (supervised and different self-supervised methods) and (b) a broad set of downstream classification datasets that vary in size, color space, and domain gap to ImageNet. The unresolved scientific need was to know whether a single pruning at pre-training yields a sparse model that preserves transfer performance across many classification targets, and if so, what sparsity levels are feasible per downstream dataset and pre-training objective. Without these quantitative thresholds, one cannot judge the tradeoff between pruning aggressiveness at pre-training time and guaranteed downstream classification utility.

Detection and segmentation impose different structural and equivariance requirements than classification (e.g., spatial localization and shift equivariance). In standard practice, detectors and segmenters are initialized from full pre-trained classifiers and then fine-tuned, but it is unclear whether pruning at pre-training preserves the spatial and representational properties required by these tasks. Prior LTH work had not comprehensively addressed transfer from pre-trained masks into detection/segmentation, nor quantified how aggressive pruning at pre-training would need to be to preserve performance on these structured tasks. Without this knowledge, attempts to reduce pre-trained model size risk breaking the downstream spatial capabilities or require task-specific re-pruning, negating amortization of pre-training cost.

If different pre-training objectives produce similar sparse subnetworks, one could expect a single pruning recipe to serve multiple pre-training paradigms; conversely, if masks differ substantially, pruning schedules and expectations about transferability must be pre-training-specific. Prior evidence for transferability of masks across pre-training regimes was lacking for convolutional backbones, and the NLP finding of transferable BERT tickets did not imply similar behavior in CV due to distinct architectures and objectives. Without characterization of mask similarity and kernel-level structure across pre-training methods, it is unclear whether a one-size-fits-all sparse pre-trained initialization is feasible or whether per-objective pruning is necessary.

Robustness of a sparse mask to small structural modifications is important for both interpretability and practical re-use. Earlier LTH findings on random initialization and early rewinding suggested that mask structure may be somewhat robust, but it was unknown whether masks derived from a pre-trained weight distribution—whose weights have already been shaped by a large-scale objective—retain that robustness. If pre-training-derived masks are fragile, then small errors or transfer conditions (e.g., reordering weights, implementation differences, or noise in pruning) could eliminate transfer benefits, limiting practicality. Establishing the relative sensitivity informs whether pruning at pre-training is a stable method for producing reusable compact initializations.

The hypothesis "train large, then compress" has been argued in NLP and generative-model contexts, but whether it benefits the quality of transferable sparse subnetworks in self-supervised CV pre-training was not established. If pruning from a large pre-trained model yields better-transferable subnetworks, then a two-stage workflow (pre-train big, then find a sparse subnetwork before fine-tuning) would be justified; otherwise, pre-training a large model solely to prune it would be wasteful. Prior to this work, there was insufficient empirical quantification in simCLR-style CV self-supervision to decide between these alternatives.

The simCLR temperature controls the contrastive loss sharpness and is known to influence learned representations; however, the degree to which temperature choices during pre-training affect the existence and transfer quality of sparse matching subnetworks was unquantified. If matching-subnetwork transferability were highly sensitive to temperature, practitioners would need to tune contrastive temperature with pruning in mind; without evidence, it is unclear how to set or default this hyperparameter when the goal is to obtain compact, transferable initializations.

LTH studies typically locate tickets at random initialization or by rewinding to early training; whether pre-trained weights offer an intrinsic advantage as the starting point for IMP—thereby producing better transferable subnetworks—was not settled. Determining this is essential to decide whether pruning should be applied before or after pre-training and whether the extra cost of pre-training before pruning is justified by improved sparse-transfer performance. Without such a comparison, recommendations about when to prune in a pre-train-then-fine-tune workflow remain speculative.

Using iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) applied at pre-trained initializations, there exist matching subnetworks (winning tickets) in ResNet-50 pre-trained models for the three studied pre-training objectives. A matching subnetwork is a mask $m\in\{0,1\}^{d_1}$ such that, for a pre-training task $\mathcal{P}$ and pre-trained weights $\theta_p$, the trained-and-evaluated subnetwork satisfies the matching condition
      $$
      \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{P}}\!\left(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{P}}\!\big(f(x;m\odot\theta_p,\gamma)\big)\right)
      \ge
      \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{P}}\!\left(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{P}}\!\big(f(x;\theta_p,\gamma)\big)\right),
      $$
      where $\odot$ denotes element-wise product and $\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{P}}$/$\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{P}}$ are the training algorithm and evaluation metric for the pre-training task. The identified winning-ticket sparsities (fraction of weights removed) on ResNet-50 pre-trained weights are: 67.23% for supervised ImageNet pre-training ($\theta_{\text{Img}}$), 59.04% for simCLR self-supervised pre-training ($\theta_{\text{sim}}$), and 95.60% for MoCo self-supervised pre-training ($\theta_{\text{MoCo}}$). These subnetworks, when trained and evaluated on their respective pre-training tasks under the same training algorithm, achieve no worse performance (within one standard deviation) than the full dense pre-trained models.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified in the derivation of Conclusion 1. The existence of winning tickets at pre-trained initializations for supervised ImageNet, simCLR, and MoCo is directly observed in Figure 2, with quantitative sparsity thresholds reported. The consistent pattern across three distinct pre-training objectives (H1) provides cross-method validation that lifts the conclusion beyond a method-specific artifact. The derivation is straightforward: Figure 2 shows the subnetwork performance within one standard deviation of the dense baseline at the claimed sparsities. The conclusion is robustly established.

nodes.title: Existence of winning tickets in pre-trained CV models (pre-training tasks)

nodes.content:
Subnetworks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) starting from pre-trained ResNet-50 weights $\theta_{\text{Img}}$ (from supervised ImageNet classification), $\theta_{\text{sim}}$ (from simCLR self-supervised pre-training), and $\theta_{\text{MoCo}}$ (from MoCo self-supervised pre-training) on ImageNet transfer universally (i.e., they are matching for multiple downstream classification datasets) up to dataset- and pre-training-specific sparsity thresholds. For each combination, the transferred subnetworks retain performance within one standard deviation of the unpruned dense fine-tuned models at the following sparsity levels (fraction of weights removed):
      - CIFAR-10: (91.41%, 91.41%, 91.41%) for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) pre-training respectively.
      - CIFAR-100: (86.58%, 86.58%, 89.26%).
      - SVHN: (91.41%, 96.48%, 93.13%).
      - Fashion-MNIST: (89.26%, 89.26%, 91.41%).
      - VisDA2017 (synthetic-to-real domain transfer): (67.23%, 59.04%, 59.04%).
      These results show that masks $m_{\mathcal{P}}$ found by IMP on pre-training task $\mathcal{P}$ (supervised ImageNet, simCLR, or MoCo) combined with the corresponding pre-trained weights $\theta_p$ serve as universal initializations for a diverse set of downstream classification tasks until dataset- and domain-specific sparsity limits are reached.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified in the derivation of Conclusion 2. The universal transfer to classification is demonstrated across five datasets that vary in size, color space, resolution, and domain gap to ImageNet (H2), which provides substantive support for generality. The sparsity thresholds are quantified per dataset, and the comparison with dense fine-tuned baselines is direct. The derived sparsity numbers may be sensitive to the within-one-standard-deviation criterion, but the overall pattern of transfer is clear and supported by multiple datasets.

nodes.title: Universal transfer of pre-training winning tickets to downstream classification tasks with quantified sparsity thresholds

nodes.content: Pre-training-derived subnetworks (consisting of mask $m_{\mathcal{P}}$ found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) on pre-training task $\mathcal{P}$ and the corresponding pre-trained ResNet-50 weights $\theta_p$ from supervised ImageNet classification ($\theta_{\text{Img}}$), simCLR ($\theta_{\text{sim}}$), or MoCo ($\theta_{\text{MoCo}}$) on ImageNet) can transfer to object detection (YOLOv4 detector) and semantic segmentation (DeepLabv3+) tasks without performance degradation up to the following sparsity levels: detection at (73.79%, 48.80%, 73.79%) for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) pre-training respectively; segmentation at (48.80%, 36.00%, 83.22%) for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) respectively. Furthermore, subnetworks found specifically on the downstream detection or segmentation tasks with the same pre-trained initialization (i.e., mask $m_{\mathcal{T}}$ found by IMP on the downstream task $\mathcal{T}$ starting from the same pre-trained weights $\theta_p$) can reach even higher sparsities while matching dense performance: detection-task-specific winning-ticket sparsities of (95.60%, 93.13%, 97.75%) and segmentation-task-specific winning-ticket sparsities of (73.79%, 67.23%, 86.58%) for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) respectively. These downstream-task-specific subnetworks outperform the transferred pre-training subnetworks by measurable margins.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified in the derivation of Conclusion 3. The transfer to detection and segmentation is demonstrated for YOLOv4 and DeepLabv3+, with quantified sparsity thresholds (H3). The success on these structurally different tasks shows that the masks preserve spatial capabilities. While the supplementary results show that transfer to other detectors (Faster R-CNN, SSD) is not always successful for simCLR, the conclusion is scoped to the tested architectures, so this does not constitute a weak point. The evidence is direct and the thresholds are clear.

nodes.title: Transferability of pre-training winning tickets to detection and segmentation with quantified sparsity and comparison to task-specific tickets

nodes.content: Masks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) on different pre-training objectives (supervised ImageNet classification, simCLR, and MoCo) using a ResNet-50 backbone are structurally heterogeneous: after five rounds of IMP (corresponding to approximately 67.23% weight sparsity), the pairwise relative mask similarity (defined as $|m_i\cap m_j|/|m_i\cup m_j|$) between any two pre-training-derived masks is below 6.55%. The masks also differ in kernel-level clustering: the number and layer-wise distribution of completely pruned (all-zero) kernels vary by pre-training objective. Subnetworks from MoCo pre-training exhibit more clustered zero-kernel patterns until extreme sparsity, and completely pruned kernels are concentrated in early residual blocks and rarely appear in later layers.

metadata.narrative: The dominant risk for Conclusion 4 is P1: the mask similarity measurements (Figure 6) are reported without evidence of reproducibility across multiple runs, placing the quantitative heterogeneity claim on uncertain ground. No highlight offsets this risk. The qualitative visualizations (Figure 7) support heterogeneity but are not quantified across replicates. If P1 were false (i.e., the similarity values are robust), the conclusion would be well-supported; but the paper does not demonstrate that robustness. The conclusion is plausible but not robustly established given the reported evidence.

nodes.title: Heterogeneity of mask structure across different pre-training objectives

nodes.content: Subnetworks obtained by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) on the CIFAR-100 downstream classification task starting from pre-trained ResNet-50 weights $\theta_{\text{Img}}$ (from supervised ImageNet classification) exhibit substantial sensitivity to structural perturbations: replacing the IMP mask with its complement $m^c$, a random pruned mask $m_r$, or a mask perturbed by randomly flipping 10% of bits significantly degrades classification performance. In contrast, subnetworks produced from random initialization ($\theta_0$, standard Kaiming initialization on CIFAR-100) or early-weight rewinding ($\theta_{5\%}$, weights from a checkpoint after 5% of CIFAR-100 training starting from $\theta_0$) are comparatively resilient to the same mask perturbations, showing only marginal performance changes. Empirically, complementary or perturbed masks applied to pre-trained weights can perform no better than IMP masks applied to random-initialized networks at the same sparsity levels.

metadata.narrative: The perturbation sensitivity analysis (Figure 8) is systematically executed across three perturbation types and three initialization types (H4), providing strong comparative evidence for the qualitative direction of the effect. The composition of risks is partially offset: H4 preempts the concern that the sensitivity might be generic to any IMP mask, but P2 identifies a confound that is not protected—the attribution of sensitivity to the mask pattern rather than to the pre-trained weight values is unsupported. Thus the empirical observation that performance degrades under perturbations is credible, but the mechanistic interpretation that pre-training-derived masks are inherently fragile is not fully isolated. The conclusion is supported for the empirical claim but the causal interpretation remains uncertain.

nodes.title: Pre-training-derived masks are more sensitive to structural perturbations than random-initialization or early-rewind masks

nodes.content: For simCLR self-supervised pre-training on ImageNet, performing iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) on a larger pre-trained backbone (ResNet-152 with simCLR weights) produces transferred subnetworks that achieve higher downstream accuracy on CIFAR-100 than subnetworks of equal remaining parameter count pruned from the smaller pre-trained backbone (ResNet-50 with simCLR weights). With the same number of remaining weights, the ResNet-152-derived masks consistently yield superior transfer performance, indicating that pruning from a larger pre-trained model can produce better transferable matching subnetworks.

metadata.narrative: The scale comparison (H5) provides a well-controlled demonstration that ResNet-152-derived subnetworks outperform ResNet-50-derived counterparts at equal remaining weight counts for simCLRv2 on CIFAR-100. The weak point P3 (pre-training version confound) limits the generality of the claim to simCLR (v1) specifically, but the conclusion's title includes "simCLR" which is not directly tested. The highlight supports the factual observation under the conditions tested. The conclusion is well-supported for the simCLRv2/CIFAR-100 regime but less so for the broader claim about simCLR pre-training.

nodes.title: Pruning from larger pre-trained models yields better transferable subnetworks (simCLR ResNet-152 > ResNet-50)

nodes.content: The contrastive-temperature hyperparameter in simCLR self-supervised pre-training on ImageNet affects the transfer quality of iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) derived subnetworks on the CIFAR-100 downstream task. For subnetworks found by IMP on the simCLR pre-training task starting from official simCLR pre-trained ResNet-50 weights, first trained at 67.23% sparsity for 10 epochs on the simCLR task and then pruned to 73.79% sparsity by IMP, downstream CIFAR-100 accuracies vary with temperature: temperatures in a moderate range $\{0.1,0.2,0.5\}$ produce similar transfer accuracies (81.81%, 81.91%, 82.22%), whereas an extreme temperature of 20.0 degrades transfer performance to 80.18%. Therefore, the simCLR temperature should be chosen moderately to preserve transferable matching-subnetwork quality.

metadata.narrative: The temperature sensitivity analysis (Table 2) is limited by a short (10-epoch) pre-training schedule applied to an already fully pre-trained model (P4), making it uncertain whether the observed pattern generalizes to standard full-length simCLR pre-training. No highlight addresses this limitation. The conclusion that temperature should be chosen moderately is plausible but not robustly supported; the evidence is insufficient to rule out that the sensitivity is an artifact of the protocol. The conclusion's practical applicability for standard simCLR pre-training remains questionable.

nodes.title: Sensitivity of matching-subnetwork transferability to simCLR temperature hyperparameter

nodes.content: Across downstream classification tasks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, and VisDA2017), iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) masks found on each downstream task starting from pre-trained initializations ($\theta_p \in \{\theta_{\text{Img}},\theta_{\text{sim}},\theta_{\text{MoCo}}\}$, ResNet-50 weights from supervised ImageNet, simCLR, or MoCo pre-training respectively) yield better transfer performance than equivalent IMP masks found from random initialization ($\theta_0$, standard Kaiming initialization on the downstream task) or early rewinding ($\theta_{5\%}$, weights from a checkpoint after 5% of downstream task training from $\theta_0$), up to relatively high sparsity levels (e.g., until approximately 67.23% sparsity). Subnetworks discovered with $\theta_0$ or $\theta_{5\%}$ are inferior on downstream tasks compared to those discovered with $\theta_p$, indicating that starting IMP at a pre-trained initialization provides a substantial advantage for finding transferable winning tickets, except at extreme sparsity where advantages diminish.

metadata.narrative: The comparison of pre-trained initialization against random and early-rewinding baselines (P5) may be affected by unequal training convergence: the random and early-rewinding subnetworks may not have been trained to saturation, potentially inflating the advantage of the pre-trained initialization. No highlight preempts this convergence confound. The conclusion is likely directionally correct—pre-trained initialization does help—but the magnitude of the claimed superiority is not rigorously established. The weak point is specific and load-bearing: if random-init tickets were trained to convergence, the gap could close at moderate sparsities, narrowing the regime where pre-trained init is strictly better.

nodes.title: Pre-trained initialization produces superior matching subnetworks compared to random initialization and early rewinding until extreme sparsity

nodes.content: In the iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) procedure applied to a ResNet-50 network initialized with pre-trained weights from supervised ImageNet classification, simCLR, and MoCov2, the pairwise relative mask similarity (intersection over union) between the masks obtained after five pruning rounds (corresponding to a weight sparsity of approximately 67.23%) is reported as a single scalar value below 6.55% for each pair of pre-training objectives, without any indication that the experiment was repeated across different random seeds or IMP orderings to quantify variability.

metadata.failure_mode: If the mask similarity measurement is not reproducible and the true typical similarity between pre-training masks were substantially higher (e.g., above 20%), then the conclusion that masks are heterogeneous would be false for the tested sparsity level. The claim that pre-training objectives produce diverse mask structures would lose its empirical basis, and the paper's interpretation that a one-size-fits-all pruning strategy is not feasible would be unsupported by the similarity evidence. The kernel-level clustering differences (Figure 7) would also lose the quantitative context that makes them striking.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that masks from different pre-training objectives are "remarkably heterogeneous" (Conclusion 4) rests primarily on the quantitative observation of low mask similarity. However, the IMP process involves randomness from SGD noise during the retraining phase between pruning rounds; the same pre-trained weights can yield different mask trajectories if the random seed or the order of data is changed. Without multiple independent replicates of the mask-similarity measurement, the reported value could be an outlier or an artifact of a particular training run. The paper does not mention the number of replicates for this analysis, nor does it provide error bars or confidence intervals. In the absence of reproducibility evidence, the measurement is not established as reliable, and the quantitative threshold of 6.55% cannot be taken as characteristic of the underlying mask structure.

nodes.title: Single-run mask similarity measurement

nodes.content: In the perturbation sensitivity analysis for CIFAR-100, the initialization types compared are pre-trained weights ($\theta_{\text{Img}}$, from supervised ImageNet classification on ResNet-50), randomly initialized weights ($\theta_0$, standard Kaiming initialization), and early-rewinding weights ($\theta_{5\%}$, weights from a checkpoint after 5% of CIFAR-100 training starting from $\theta_0$). The weight values across these initializations differ drastically in structure: $\theta_{\text{Img}}$ contains learned convolutional filters that encode semantic visual features (edges, textures, object parts), whereas $\theta_0$ and $\theta_{5\%}$ consist of near-random or partially trained weights that lack hierarchical feature structure. The same mask perturbation (e.g., using the complementary mask $m^c$) therefore removes fundamentally different weight sets in each case: from $\theta_{\text{Img}}$ it removes functional units that contribute to performance, while from $\theta_0/\theta_{5\%}$ it removes weights that have not yet formed structured representations.

metadata.failure_mode: If the sensitivity difference is driven by the weight values rather than the mask pattern, then the conclusion that "pre-training-derived masks are more sensitive to structural perturbations" conflates cause and would need to be reframed to "pre-trained weights are more sensitive to any structural perturbation of their mask." The practical implication that pre-training masks are fragile and require careful handling is not invalidated, but the theoretical implication about mask structure (which differentiates pre-training tickets from random-init tickets) is unsupported. The comparison with random init and early rewinding would no longer isolate mask properties, weakening the claim's distinctiveness.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper attributes the dramatic performance drop under mask perturbations (complementary, random, 10% flip) to the "more sensitive" nature of pre-training-derived masks. However, the experimental design conflates the effect of the mask pattern with the effect of the weight values being masked. The same perturbation applied on different weight distributions is not an apples-to-apples comparison of mask sensitivity; it also tests the sensitivity of the weight distribution itself. A more controlled test would compare mask perturbations on different masks applied to the same set of pre-trained weights (e.g., IMP mask vs. IMP mask on randomly shuffled pre-trained weights). Without such control, the claim that the mask structure (as opposed to the weight values) is more sensitive is not causally supported. The observed degradation could equally be explained by the fact that any non-optimal pruning of pre-trained weights destroys valuable learned structure.

nodes.title: Weight-value confound in perturbation analysis

nodes.content: The ablation comparing pre-training scale (ResNet-152 vs. ResNet-50) uses models pre-trained with simCLRv2 (which adds a self-distillation stage after standard contrastive learning) rather than the original simCLR (v1) pre-training used for the main experiments. The simCLRv2 procedure includes an additional step where a teacher model trained via contrastive learning is used to distill its representations into a student network, modifying the final weight distribution. The downstream transfer evaluation is performed only on CIFAR-100, and no other downstream task (classification datasets, detection, segmentation) is tested for the scale comparison.

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed advantage of ResNet-152 over ResNet-50 is due to the simCLRv2 training protocol (specifically the distillation phase) rather than to the larger model capacity, then the conclusion that "pruning from larger pre-trained models yields better transferable subnetworks" would not be valid for the original simCLR (v1) pre-training. Practitioners using simCLR (v1) might not see the same benefit. Additionally, if the advantage does not transfer to other downstream tasks beyond CIFAR-100, the claim's practical scope would be narrower than implied.
metadata.weakness_reason: The conclusion states "For simCLR self-supervised pre-training, performing IMP on a larger pre-trained backbone (ResNet-152) produces transferred subnetworks that achieve higher downstream accuracy on CIFAR-100 than subnetworks of equal remaining parameter count pruned from the smaller pre-trained backbone (ResNet-50)." However, the evidence uses simCLRv2, which is a distinct training method from simCLR (v1). The scale advantage could be partly or wholly due to the distillation component of v2 rather than model scale alone. Furthermore, the evaluation on a single downstream dataset (CIFAR-100) leaves it open whether the advantage holds for other tasks; the conclusion does not claim generality beyond CIFAR-100, but the title of the conclusion in the inference unit ("Pruning from larger pre-trained models yields better transferable subnetworks (simCLR ResNet-152 > ResNet-50)") could be read as a general statement about simCLR pre-training. The weak point is that the pre-training version confound prevents isolating the scale effect for simCLR specifically.

nodes.title: simCLRv2 vs simCLR and single-task evaluation in scale ablation

nodes.content: The temperature-ablation experiment uses subnetworks trained on the simCLR pre-training task for only 10 additional epochs from the official simCLR pre-trained weights (which were trained for hundreds of epochs) before pruning to the target sparsity. The pre-training phase for the official simCLR ResNet-50 involves 800 or 1000 epochs of contrastive learning; the short extra training (10 epochs) may not allow the contrastive-loss temperature effect to manifest in the same way as it would during full pre-training. Furthermore, the subnetworks are evaluated at a single sparsity level (73.79%) on a single downstream dataset (CIFAR-100).

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed temperature sensitivity is an artifact of the short (10-epoch) pre-training schedule, then the recommendation to choose moderate temperatures (e.g., 0.1-0.5) for practitioners seeking transferable subnetworks may be incorrect when using standard full-length simCLR pre-training. The degradation at extreme temperatures (e.g., 20.0) might disappear or reverse under full pre-training. The quantitative accuracies reported in Table 2 would not reflect the behavior of subnetworks obtained from fully pre-trained models, and Conclusion 7 would be unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: The temperature hyperparameter's effect on learned representations during simCLR pre-training is known to be mediated by the length of training, with the temperature influencing the contrastive loss distribution over time. Using only 10 epochs of continued pretraining from an already converged model may produce a different temperature sensitivity profile than starting from scratch or from the full pre-training schedule. The paper's conclusion that "the simCLR temperature should be chosen moderately to preserve transferable matching-subnetwork quality" is based on this limited-duration pre-training. It is not established that the same pattern holds when temperature is varied during the full pre-training phase. Additionally, the test on a single sparsity level and dataset means the conclusion may not generalize to other sparsity regimes or downstream tasks.

nodes.title: Short pre-training schedule in temperature ablation

nodes.content: In the comparison of subnetworks from pre-trained initialization ($\theta_{\text{Img}}$) versus random initialization ($\theta_0$) and early-rewinding ($\theta_{5\%}$) on the CIFAR-100 downstream classification task, the training protocol uses an identical number of epochs (182) and learning rate schedule for all three initializations. For random initialization, 182 epochs of SGD training from scratch on CIFAR-100 may not be sufficient for the subnetwork to reach its maximal accuracy, especially at moderate to high sparsities where optimization is harder. For pre-trained initialization, the same 182 epochs of fine-tuning start from a strong feature extractor and are typically adequate. The paper does not verify that the random-initialization and early-rewinding baselines have converged (e.g., by extending training until validation loss plateaus or by using a learning rate schedule tailored to from-scratch training).

metadata.failure_mode: If the random-initialization subnetworks were trained to convergence (either with more epochs or a refined schedule), their performance might increase substantially, especially at moderate sparsities (e.g., 40%-70%). This could reduce or eliminate the performance gap with pre-trained-initialization subnetworks, undermining Conclusion 8's claim of superiority. The conclusion would then need to be revised to state that pre-trained initialization provides better performance under a fixed training budget (which is practically useful) but not necessarily better final achievable performance. The distinction is important for understanding whether pre-training is required to find good tickets or whether longer training suffices.
metadata.weakness_reason: The claim that pre-trained initialization produces superior matching subnetworks (Conclusion 8) depends on a fair comparison between initializations. However, the training budget (epochs, learning rate schedule) was designed for fine-tuning, not for from-scratch training. ResNet-50 typically requires more than 182 epochs from scratch on CIFAR-100 to reach peak performance (e.g., 300-600 epochs are common), and the standard schedule for from-scratch training often involves a lower initial learning rate or a different decay pattern. The paper does not show that the random-init and early-rewind subnetworks have been trained to saturation; the observed gap may therefore be inflated by insufficient training rather than reflecting a fundamental difference in subnetwork quality. This is a common issue in LTH comparisons (as noted in prior literature), and the paper would need additional experiments (e.g., training to convergence, tuning hyperparameters per init) to establish the superiority conclusively.

nodes.title: Unequal convergence in initialization comparison

nodes.content: Iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) applied to ResNet-50 weights pre-trained on ImageNet via three different objectives—supervised classification, simCLR contrastive learning, and MoCov2 momentum contrastive learning—consistently yields matching subnetworks (defined as subnetworks whose performance after training on the pre-training task is within one standard deviation of the dense model's performance under the same training algorithm). The observed winning-ticket sparsities are 67.23% for supervised, 59.04% for simCLR, and 95.60% for MoCov2. The consistency across one supervised and two contrastive self-supervised methods, which employ different loss functions (cross-entropy, InfoNCE, contrastive loss with momentum encoder) and training dynamics, indicates that the existence of winning tickets at pre-trained initializations is a general property of pre-trained convolutional networks, not an artifact of a specific objective.

metadata.credit: This finding preempts the concern that winning tickets might exist only for supervised pre-training or only for a particular self-supervised method, which would limit the practical relevance of the phenomenon. By demonstrating matching subnetworks for three distinct pre-training objectives, the paper underwrites Conclusion 1's claim that "there exist matching subnetworks in pre-trained CV models" as a robust phenomenon across pre-training regimes. The credit scope is qualitative direction and generalization: without this consistency, a skeptical reader could dismiss the existence as method-specific. The observation that MoCov2 supports much higher sparsity (95.60%) than simCLR (59.04%) further shows that the existence is not uniform but still present across the board.

nodes.title: Consistent winning-ticket existence across three pre-training objectives

nodes.content: For ResNet-50 pre-trained on ImageNet via supervised classification, simCLR, and MoCov2, the same IMP masks found on the pre-training task are applied to five downstream classification datasets without modification: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, and VisDA2017. Across these datasets, which vary in image resolution (32x32 to 224x224), color channels (RGB, grayscale), number of classes (10 to 100), and domain gap to ImageNet (natural images, synthetic images for VisDA), the transferred subnetworks maintain performance within one standard deviation of the fine-tuned dense model at sparsity levels between 59.04% and 96.48% (depending on the dataset and pre-training objective). The sparsity thresholds for successful transfer are quantified per dataset, providing a practical guideline.

metadata.credit: This finding preempts the concern that transfer might only work for datasets that are very similar to ImageNet (e.g., other natural-image benchmarks at 224x224). By including SVHN (digit recognition), Fashion-MNIST (grayscale product images), and the synthetic-to-real domain adaptation benchmark VisDA2017, the paper shows that the transferred subnetworks are effective even under considerable domain shift. This underwrites Conclusion 2's claim of "universal transfer" (within the tested set) by providing evidence across a deliberately heterogeneous selection of downstream classification tasks. The credit scope is generalization and regime-bounded support: the conclusion gains specific credibility for the diversity of evaluated tasks, which is a substantive design choice beyond testing only one or two similar datasets.

nodes.title: Transfer across diverse classification datasets

nodes.content: For ResNet-50 pre-trained weights, pre-training-derived IMP masks transfer to object detection (YOLOv4 on Pascal VOC) and semantic segmentation (DeepLabv3+ on Pascal VOC) without performance degradation (within one standard deviation of the dense fine-tuned model) at the following sparsities: YOLOv4 detection at (73.79%, 48.80%, 73.79%) and DeepLabv3+ segmentation at (48.80%, 36.00%, 83.22%) for supervised ImageNet, simCLR, and MoCov2 pre-training respectively. Detection requires location shift equivariance and segmentation requires dense per-pixel prediction, both of which have different invariance properties than classification. The successful transfer demonstrates that the pre-training-derived masks preserve the spatial and representational capabilities needed for these structurally more demanding tasks.

metadata.credit: This finding preempts the concern that pruning at the pre-training stage might destroy the spatial localization and fine-grained feature representations required by detection and segmentation—a non-trivial risk given that classification does not require precise spatial information. By demonstrating matching performance on a one-stage detector (YOLOv4) and an encoder-decoder segmenter (DeepLabv3+), the paper underwrites Conclusion 3's claim that pre-training-derived masks can transfer to structured prediction tasks. The credit scope is qualitative direction and regime-bounded support: the conclusion is supported for the specific detection/segmentation architectures tested, and the sparsity thresholds are quantified.

nodes.title: Transfer to detection and segmentation

nodes.content: On the CIFAR-100 downstream task, the paper compares the effect of three types of mask perturbation—complementary mask (m^c), random pruned mask (m_r), and mask with 10% of bits flipped (m + Δm_10%)—on subnetworks obtained from three initialization types: pre-trained θ_Img, random θ_0, and early-rewinding θ_5%. For the pre-trained initialization, all three perturbations cause a substantial performance drop (e.g., accuracy falls from approximately 82% to below 20% with the complementary mask). For the random and early-rewinding initializations, the same perturbations produce only marginal changes (within a few percentage points). This controlled experiment across three perturbation types and three initializations provides a systematic characterization of sensitivity that goes beyond a single comparison.

metadata.credit: This finding preempts the concern that the sensitivity might be an artifact of the particular perturbation chosen or might also hold for other initializations (which would make it a generic property of IMP masks). By testing three different perturbation types and showing that the sensitivity is much larger for pre-trained initialization, the paper establishes that pre-training-derived masks are genuinely more fragile in a qualitative sense. The three-fold replication (complement, random, flip) across three init types strengthens the conclusion beyond a single comparison. The credit scope is qualitative direction and comparative differentiation: the conclusion that pre-training masks are more sensitive is empirically robust across multiple perturbation definitions.

nodes.title: Systematic perturbation analysis across three perturbation types

nodes.content: For simCLRv2 pre-trained models on ResNet-50 and ResNet-152, IMP is applied to both and the resulting subnetworks are pruned to various parameter budgets. At the same number of remaining weights (from approximately 1 million to 5 million), the subnetworks derived from the larger ResNet-152 achieve consistently higher downstream accuracy on CIFAR-100 than those from ResNet-50 (e.g., at 2.5M remaining weights: ~77% vs ~74%). The comparison is controlled for the number of remaining weights, the pre-training method (simCLRv2), the IMP procedure, and the downstream fine-tuning protocol.

metadata.credit: This finding preempts the concern that the advantage of larger pre-trained models might be due simply to having more parameter budget rather than a genuine benefit of "pruning from larger." By comparing at equal remaining weight counts, the paper demonstrates that the larger model's initial parameter space yields a better subnetwork at the same size. This underwrites Conclusion 6's claim that "pruning from larger pre-trained models yields better transferable subnetworks" for the simCLRv2/CIFAR-100 setting. The credit scope is regime-bounded support and quantitative direction: the advantage is not assumed from prior work but directly measured in this controlled setting.

nodes.title: Controlled scale comparison at equal remaining weights

steps.reasoning: Define the network and subnetworks used throughout: let $f(x;\theta,\gamma)$ be the output of a ResNet-50 model with parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1}$ (excluding the first convolution layer) and task-specific parameters $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{d_2}$ on input image $x$; let a pruning binary mask be $m \in \{0,1\}^{d_1}$ and denote element-wise product by $\odot$, so a subnetwork is $f(x;m \odot \theta,\gamma)$.

State the matching-subnetwork criterion used to identify winning tickets: a subnetwork $f(x;m\odot\theta,\gamma)$ is matching for a task $\mathcal{T}$ if its evaluation after training, denoted by $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}\!\big(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}\!\big(f(x;m\odot\theta,\gamma)\big)\big)$, satisfies the inequality
$$
\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(f(x;m\odot\theta,\gamma)\right)\right)
\ge
\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(f(x;\theta_p,\gamma)\right)\right),
$$
where $\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}$ is the training algorithm for task $\mathcal{T}$ and $\theta_p$ denotes the pre-trained weights used as the reference dense model; this formal inequality is the operational definition of a matching subnetwork used in the experiments.

Specify pre-trained initializations and pre-training tasks: let $\theta_{\text{Img}}$ denote supervised ImageNet pre-trained ResNet-50 weights, $\theta_{\text{sim}}$ denote simCLR pre-trained ResNet-50 weights, and $\theta_{\text{MoCo}}$ denote MoCo (MoCov2) pre-trained ResNet-50 weights; the search for matching subnetworks is performed starting from each respective $\theta_p \in \{\theta_{\text{Img}},\theta_{\text{sim}},\theta_{\text{MoCo}}\}$.

Describe the pruning procedure used to find subnetworks: apply iterative magnitude pruning (IMP), which (a) initializes a mask $m=1^{d_1}$ and the chosen pre-trained weights $\theta_p$, (b) repeatedly trains the current masked network $f(x;m\odot\theta_p,\gamma)$ to completion on the pre-training task using the same training algorithm $\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{P}}$, (c) prunes the globally smallest-magnitude 20% of remaining weights and updates $m$, and (d) repeats until the desired sparsity is reached; this iterative pruning procedure and its use for finding matching subnetworks follows the standard IMP routine.
[31]

State the empirical experimental setup for pre-training used to evaluate matching: pre-training experiments are conducted on ImageNet with the official pre-trained ResNet-50 for supervised ImageNet and publicly released pre-trained ResNet-50s for simCLR and MoCov2; the evaluation metric for supervised pre-training is Top-1 accuracy as in standard ImageNet evaluation (Table 1 provides pre-training hyperparameters such as number of epochs and optimizer settings).
Fig. 2
Table 1

Present the empirical finding that IMP at pre-trained initializations yields matching subnetworks for the pre-training tasks: after applying the IMP procedure starting from each pre-trained initialization $\theta_p$, the authors find subnetworks whose trained-and-evaluated performance on their respective pre-training tasks meets or exceeds the dense pre-trained models' performance (using the matching criterion above, counted as within one standard deviation to account for random variation), with the identified winning-ticket sparsities being 67.23% for supervised ImageNet ($\theta_{\text{Img}}$), 59.04% for simCLR ($\theta_{\text{sim}}$), and 95.60% for MoCo ($\theta_{\text{MoCo}}$); these numerical sparsities are reported from the ImageNet pre-training performance curves and summarized in the text.
Fig. 2

Record the operational decision used to count a subnetwork as a winning ticket in practice: to account for run-to-run variability, a subnetwork is considered a winning ticket if its evaluation is within one standard deviation of the unpruned dense model's evaluation under the same training algorithm $\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{P}}$ and evaluation function $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{P}}$; this practical tie-breaking is applied when declaring the subnetworks at the sparsities reported above to be matching.

Treat as given the established existence of winning tickets at pre-trained initializations for the three pre-training objectives (the result just established: there exist masks $m_{\mathcal{P}}$ found by IMP at pre-trained weights $\theta_p \in \{\theta_{\text{Img}},\theta_{\text{sim}},\theta_{\text{MoCo}}\}$ that are matching on their corresponding pre-training tasks).

Define the transfer question and evaluation convention: for a downstream classification task $\mathcal{T}$ (e.g., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, VisDA2017), consider using the pre-training-derived subnetwork $f(x;m_{\mathcal{P}}\odot\theta_p,\gamma_{\mathcal{T}})$ (where $\gamma_{\mathcal{T}}$ denotes task-specific modules such as final linear layers) and train it with the downstream training algorithm $\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}$; declare the transferred subnetwork to be matching for the downstream task if its evaluation $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}\!\big(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}\!\big(f(x;m_{\mathcal{P}}\odot\theta_p,\gamma_{\mathcal{T}})\big)\big)$ is within one standard deviation of the unpruned dense fine-tuned model $\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{T}}\!\big(\mathcal{A}_t^{\mathcal{T}}\!\big(f(x;\theta_p,\gamma_{\mathcal{T}})\big)\big)$.

Describe the experimental procedure for measuring transfer: for each pre-training-derived mask $(m_{\mathcal{P}},\theta_p)$, transfer the masked pre-trained backbone to downstream classification tasks by attaching task-specific classification heads and fine-tuning using the downstream training schedules and hyperparameters specified in Table 1 (e.g., CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100: 182 epochs, batch size 256, learning rate 0.1 with scheduled decays), then evaluate test-set accuracy and compute standard deviations across three independent runs to judge the within-one-standard-deviation matching criterion.
Fig. 3
Table 1

Report the empirical transfer threshold for the synthetic-to-real domain transfer dataset VisDA2017: the transferred subnetworks $(m_{\mathcal{P}},\theta_p)$ retain performance within one standard deviation of dense fine-tuned models up to sparsities 67.23%, 59.04%, 59.04% for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) pre-training respectively; this required lower sparsity (i.e., more remaining parameters) compared to natural-image datasets because of the domain gap between synthetic and real images.
Fig. 4

Conclude the universal-transfer claim in operational terms: because the pre-training-derived masks $(m_{\mathcal{P}},\theta_p)$, when fine-tuned on a diverse set of downstream classification datasets, achieve no worse performance than dense fine-tuned models (within one standard deviation) up to the dataset- and pre-training-specific sparsity thresholds listed above, these pre-training-derived masks serve as universal initializations for classification downstreams until dataset- and domain-specific sparsity limits are reached.
Fig. 3

Begin from the upstream result that IMP produces winning tickets at pre-trained initializations for the three pre-training objectives (the existence of $(m_{\mathcal{P}},\theta_p)$ matching on pre-training tasks is treated as established).

Describe the downstream tasks and backbones used for transfer-to-detection and transfer-to-segmentation experiments: object detection experiments use YOLOv4 with a ResNet-50 backbone and semantic segmentation uses DeepLabv3+ with a ResNet-50 backbone; the first convolution layer and task-specific heads are not pruned, and standard detection/segmentation training schedules and evaluation metrics (AP, AP₅₀, AP₇₅ for detection; mIOU for segmentation) are used as described in Table 1 and the main experimental protocol.
Fig. 5
Table 1

Report the sparsity levels up to which pre-training-derived subnetworks transfer to detection and segmentation without performance degradation: the transferred subnetworks $f(x;m_{\mathcal{P}}\odot\theta_p,\cdot)$ successfully transfer to detection and segmentation tasks at sparsities (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) equal to detection: (73.79%, 48.80%, 73.79%) and segmentation: (48.80%, 36.00%, 83.22%), as observed from the performance-versus-sparsity curves for YOLOv4 detection and DeepLabv3+ segmentation.
Fig. 5

Describe the alternative of finding subnetworks specifically on the downstream tasks: for each downstream task $\mathcal{T}$ (detection or segmentation), perform IMP starting from the same pre-trained initialization $\theta_p$ but pruning during training on the downstream task to yield task-specific subnetworks $(m_{\mathcal{T}},\theta_p)$; these are evaluated as a performance upper bound for IMP subnetworks transferred from pre-training.
[31]

Report the downstream-task-specific winning-ticket sparsities and compare to transferred pre-training masks: detection-task-specific winning-ticket sparsities (i.e., matching subnetworks found by IMP on the detection task with pre-trained initializations) are observed to be (95.60%, 93.13%, 97.75%) for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) respectively; segmentation-task-specific winning-ticket sparsities are observed at (73.79%, 67.23%, 86.58%) for (ImageNet, simCLR, MoCo) respectively. These task-specific subnetworks consistently achieve at least as good and often strictly better detection/segmentation performance than the transferred pre-training subnetworks at the same sparsity levels.
Fig. 5

Conclude the comparative performance statement: because the downstream-task-specific subnetworks $(m_{\mathcal{T}},\theta_p)$ (found by IMP on the downstream task) can reach much higher sparsities while matching dense task performance (the numbers in the previous step) and empirically outperform the transferred pre-training subnetworks $(m_{\mathcal{P}},\theta_p)$ by measurable margins in the detection/segmentation evaluations, the authors conclude that although pre-training-derived subnetworks can transfer to detection and segmentation, task-specific IMP on the downstream task yields even sparser matching subnetworks that give better task performance.

Treat as known the procedure that IMP is applied to pre-trained initializations $\theta_{\text{Img}}$, $\theta_{\text{sim}}$, $\theta_{\text{MoCo}}$ to produce masks $m_{\text{Img}}$, $m_{\text{sim}}$, $m_{\text{MoCo}}$; the current analysis compares structural properties of these masks.

Define the quantitative measure of mask similarity used: for two Hamming masks $m_i,m_j \in \{0,1\}^{d_1}$, define their relative mask similarity as $\frac{|m_i \cap m_j|}{|m_i \cup m_j|}$, where $|\,\cdot\,|$ denotes the count of ones (i.e., the cardinality of the support), so the ratio measures the fraction of positions in common among the positions that are nonzero in at least one of the masks.

Report the empirical relative-similarity observation after five rounds of IMP: masks found on different pre-training objectives are remarkably heterogeneous — after five-round IMP the pairwise relative mask similarity between any two of $m_{\text{Img}}$, $m_{\text{sim}}$, $m_{\text{MoCo}}$ is below 6.55%; this numerical bound is reported directly from the relative-similarity plot and the accompanying text discussing Fig. 6.
Fig. 6

Introduce the concept of completely pruned (all-zero) kernels and explain the kernel-level clustering statistic: for convolutional kernels organized per layer, a kernel is counted as completely pruned (a "zero kernel") if all weights in that kernel are zero under the mask; counting the number and layer-wise distribution of zero kernels provides a coarse measure of how pruning clusters weights into structured all-zero units.

Report kernel-clustering empirical differences across pre-trainings: the number and layer-wise distribution of completely pruned kernels vary by pre-training objective — subnetworks derived from MoCo pre-training exhibit more clustered zero-kernel patterns (i.e., more completely pruned kernels) than those from ImageNet and simCLR up to high sparsity levels, until extreme sparsity (e.g., 95.60%) where behaviors converge; this observation comes from the bottom panel of Fig. 6 and the text commentary.
Fig. 6

Report spatial (layer-wise) localization of zero kernels from kernel-wise visualizations: kernel-wise heatmap visualizations for subnetworks at 79.03% sparsity show that completely pruned (all-zero) kernels are mainly clustered in early residual blocks (denoted B1 to B4 in the ResNet-50 backbone visualization) and appear rarely in later layers; among the three pre-training types, the MoCo-derived subnetwork shows the most dispersed distribution of completely pruned kernels; these qualitative and quantitative patterns are documented in Fig. 7 and the accompanying text.
Fig. 7

Conclude the heterogeneity claim: because the three mask sources exhibit low pairwise overlap (below 6.55%) after iterative pruning, different counts and distributions of completely pruned kernels (with MoCo showing more clustering until extreme sparsity), and distinct kernel-wise visual patterns (zero kernels concentrated in early blocks), the masks found by IMP on different pre-training objectives are structurally heterogeneous in both overall support and kernel-level clustering.

Take as established that IMP can be run from different initializations: the pre-trained initialization $\theta_{\text{Img}}$, the random initialization $\theta_0$, and an early rewinding initialization $\theta_{5\%}$ (weights saved after 5% of training), and that masks can be found by applying IMP on a downstream task such as CIFAR-100 to yield a mask $m_{\text{CIFAR-100}}$ for a given initialization.

Define the structural-perturbation mask variants used in experiments: given an IMP mask $m \in \{0,1\}^{d_1}$, define its complement $m^c$ by $m \cap m^c = \emptyset$ and $m \cup m^c = \mathbf{1}$; define a randomly pruned mask $m_r$ as a mask that randomly retains the same number of weights as $m$ but at random positions; define a perturbed mask $m + \Delta m_{10\%}$ formed by randomly flipping 10% of ones to zeros and 10% of zeros to ones in $m$.

Describe the perturbation-sensitivity experimental procedure: for CIFAR-100, find IMP masks $m_{\text{CIFAR-100}}$ using each initialization $\theta \in \{\theta_0,\theta_{5\%},\theta_{\text{Img}}\}$, then evaluate the downstream classification performance of subnetworks obtained by applying $m_{\text{CIFAR-100}}$, $m_{\text{CIFAR-100}}^c$, $m_r$, and $m_{\text{CIFAR-100}}+\Delta m_{10\%}$ to the corresponding initialization and retraining under identical training recipes; average curves over three independent runs to obtain empirical stability/error estimates.
Fig. 8

Report the empirical sensitivity contrast between initializations: subnetworks found from random initialization $\theta_0$ or early rewinding $\theta_{5\%}$ are resilient to structural perturbations — performance differences across the mask variants ($m$, $m^c$, $m_r$, $m+\Delta m_{10\%}$) are marginal; in contrast, subnetworks found from the pre-trained initialization $\theta_{\text{Img}}$ are sensitive: replacing the IMP mask with its complement, with a random mask, or with a 10%-bit-flip perturbed mask substantially degrades downstream CIFAR-100 accuracy relative to the original IMP mask applied to $\theta_{\text{Img}}$, as shown in the comparison curves.
Fig. 8

State the cross-initialization empirical comparison that motivates the conclusion: applying complementary or otherwise perturbed masks to pre-trained weights (for example, $(m^c_{\text{CIFAR-100}},\theta_{\text{Img}})$) yields performance that can be no better than applying the original IMP mask to a random-initialized network (for example, $(m_{\text{CIFAR-100}},\theta_0)$) at the same sparsity; this observation is explicitly reported in the right subfigure of Fig. 8 and in the text summary.
Fig. 8

Record an auxiliary observation about sparsity regimes: the pre-trained initialization consistently benefits accuracy of random-pruned subnetworks until a relatively high sparsity level (e.g., about 67.23% sparsity), beyond which the performance of randomly pruned subnetworks becomes insensitive to initialization; this supports the more general claim that pre-training-derived masks are more structurally fragile to perturbations than masks from random or early-rewind initializations, and that pre-training structural advantages diminish at extreme sparsity.
Fig. 8

Start from the experimental setup that simCLR pre-trained models of different backbone sizes (ResNet-50 and ResNet-152) are available: specifically, simCLRv2 pre-trained ResNet-152 and ResNet-50 models are used so as to fairly compare large- and small-scale pre-trained backbones for the simCLR pre-training regime.
[11]

Describe the pruning-and-transfer evaluation protocol used for the comparison: perform IMP on each simCLR pre-trained backbone (ResNet-50 and ResNet-152) to obtain masks that retain various numbers of remaining weights (i.e., different sparsity levels); then transfer these masked pre-trained backbones to a downstream classification task (CIFAR-100) and evaluate the downstream test accuracy as a function of the number of remaining weights, comparing the two backbone sources at equal remaining-parameter counts.
Fig. 9

Report the empirical comparison result: with the same number of remaining weights, subnetworks pruned from simCLR pre-trained ResNet-152 achieve consistently higher CIFAR-100 accuracy than subnetworks pruned from simCLR pre-trained ResNet-50 across the range of sparsities examined; this consistent superiority is shown in the transfer-performance-versus-remaining-weights plot.
Fig. 9

Conclude the pruning-from-larger-model advantage statement: because pruning (IMP) performed on the larger simCLR pre-trained backbone (ResNet-152) produces subnetworks that, for any fixed remaining-parameter budget, transfer to CIFAR-100 with higher accuracy than subnetworks pruned from the smaller simCLR pre-trained backbone (ResNet-50), the authors conclude that pruning from a larger pre-trained model can produce better transferable matching subnetworks in the simCLR regime.

Treat as given the simCLR pre-training context and that simCLR uses a temperature-scaling hyperparameter in its contrastive loss; denote this temperature parameter by $T$ (a scalar positive real number) and note it affects the pre-training objective and thus the quality of resulting pre-trained weights and subsequently IMP-derived masks.

Describe the experimental procedure used to study temperature sensitivity: start from subnetworks at 67.23% sparsity trained for 10 epochs on the simCLR pre-training task using different temperature values $T$, then prune these subnetworks further by IMP to 73.79% sparsity, and finally fine-tune and evaluate the resulting subnetworks $(m_{\text{sim}},\theta_{\text{sim}})$ on the downstream CIFAR-100 classification task; record downstream accuracy for each temperature.

Report the numerical results from the temperature ablation table: for subnetworks with 73.79% sparsity transferred to CIFAR-100, the recorded accuracies are (by temperature $T$): $T=0.1 \mapsto 81.81\%$, $T=0.2 \mapsto 81.91\%$, $T=0.5 \mapsto 82.22\%$, $T=1.0 \mapsto 81.24\%$, $T=2.0 \mapsto 80.76\%$, $T=10.0 \mapsto 81.46\%$, and $T=20.0 \mapsto 80.18\%$; these numbers are reproduced from the tabulated results.
Table 2

State the empirical conclusion about temperature selection: temperatures in a moderate range (specifically $T \in \{0.1,0.2,0.5\}$) produce similar and near-optimal downstream transfer accuracies (81.81%, 81.91%, 82.22%), whereas an extreme temperature such as $T=20.0$ degrades transfer performance (80.18%); therefore, choosing $T$ in a moderate range preserves transferable matching-subnetwork quality for simCLR.
Table 2

Start from the experimental contrast that IMP can be performed with pre-trained initializations $\theta_p \in \{\theta_{\text{Img}},\theta_{\text{sim}},\theta_{\text{MoCo}}\}$, with random initialization $\theta_0$, or with an early-rewind initialization $\theta_{5\%}$, and that downstream transfer performance is measured by fine-tuning the resulting $(m,\theta)$ pairs on downstream classification tasks.

Describe the empirical comparison methodology: for each initialization type, find IMP masks at a range of sparsities and evaluate downstream classification accuracy (e.g., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, VisDA2017); compare performance curves of $(m,\theta_p)$ versus $(m,\theta_0)$ and $(m,\theta_{5\%})$ to determine which initialization yields better transferable matching subnetworks at each sparsity.
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Report the core empirical observation about superiority of pre-trained initialization: across downstream classification tasks, IMP masks found with pre-trained initializations $\theta_p$ yield better transfer performance than equivalent IMP masks found from random initialization $\theta_0$ or early rewinding $\theta_{5\%}$ up to relatively high sparsity levels (for example, up to approximately 67.23% sparsity the advantage is clear); this result is summarized in the classification transfer plots and in the textual summary that subnetworks with $\theta_0$ and $\theta_{5\%}$ are inferior on all downstream tasks compared to subnetworks with $\theta_p$.
Fig. 3

Record the caveat about extreme sparsity: when sparsity becomes extreme (very high fraction of weights removed, e.g., beyond the approximate 67.23% regime cited), the advantages of starting from pre-trained initialization diminish and in some measures the differences between initializations become small; this behavior is explicitly reported in the CIFAR-100 robustness/perturbation experiments and general transfer curves.
Fig. 8

Conclude the practical recommendation and summarizing claim: because IMP masks found from pre-trained initializations $\theta_p$ consistently yield superior downstream transfer performance compared to masks found from $\theta_0$ or $\theta_{5\%}$ across a large range of sparsities relevant to transfer (and up to about 67.23% sparsity in many reported comparisons), the authors conclude that pre-trained initialization produces superior matching subnetworks for downstream classification until extreme sparsity regimes where the advantage diminishes.
Fig. 3

open_questions.content: The study leaves several empirically and practically relevant issues open. First, the generality beyond the evaluated architectures, datasets, and pruning protocol: whether other backbone families (e.g., Vision Transformers), other self-supervised objectives, different IMP schedules, or structured pruning schemes yield the same existence, sparsity thresholds, and mask properties remains unresolved. Second, hardware- and runtime implications are not established: how the identified unstructured sparse matching subnetworks translate into actual end-to-end training or inference speedups on realistic accelerators (including whether kernel-level clustering suffices for practical gains) requires further evaluation. Third, the variability across detector architectures observed in supplementary experiments (e.g., differing transfer success between YOLOv4 vs Faster R-CNN/SSD for some pre-training regimes) indicates that the interplay between detector design and pre-training-derived masks is not fully understood. Fourth, the limits of sparsity for universal transfer across very large-scale downstream tasks or tasks requiring stronger spatial reasoning are not precisely characterized. Finally, while several ablations (pre-training scale, temperature) were explored, systematic principles for choosing pre-training and pruning hyperparameters to optimally produce universally transferable tickets are still lacking; these present concrete directions for future work.

paper.authors: Tianlong Chen | Jonathan Frankle | Shiyu Chang | Sijia Liu | Yang Zhang | Michael Carbin | Zhangyang Wang
paper.en_title: The Lottery Tickets Hypothesis for Supervised and Self-supervised Pre-training in Computer Vision Models
